insights.title: Your iron and magnesium may be lowering how much thyroid medicine you absorb
insights.found: Iron, calcium, magnesium and some foods reduce how much levothyroxine your body takes up when they are taken close to the tablet.
insights.why: You take your tablet at about 07:00 and, on iron days, your iron bisglycinate with breakfast about 20 minutes later. Your TSH dropped while your iron was paused and rose again after you restarted it.
insights.means: On iron days your body may be getting less medicine than on other days - one possible reason your TSH has moved so much since late 2024.
insights.do: Keep your tablet on an empty stomach with water, and take iron and magnesium at least 4 hours away from it, for example iron with dinner. Ask your doctor before changing anything.
insights.expected: A steadier TSH at your next tests is the likely result if timing was the problem. Bedtime and morning dosing work equally well in a systematic review.
insights.helps: A simple timing change could steady your thyroid results.

insights.title: Your iron stores are worth re-checking now
insights.found: Iron deficiency can come back, and in people with thyroid conditions it is sometimes linked to absorption problems such as coeliac disease or autoimmune gastritis.
insights.why: You were treated for iron-deficiency anaemia in 2024, paused iron in December 2025 and restarted it in April 2026 when hair shedding began. There is no ferritin or blood count on record since 2024.
insights.means: You may be taking iron you no longer need, or not enough. Both matter, because iron also changes how your thyroid tablet is absorbed.
insights.do: Your panel includes ferritin, transferrin saturation and a full blood count. Skip your iron for 24 hours before the test so the result reflects your stores.
insights.expected: A clear answer on whether to continue, change or stop your iron.
insights.helps: Tells you whether your iron is still needed, and how much.

insights.title: Some of your symptoms are worth checking against your dose
insights.found: Anxiety, a racing heart and poor sleep linked to levothyroxine happen mainly when the dose is a little too high (TSH pushed low). At the right dose, trials show no difference from placebo.
insights.why: In January 2026 your TSH was 0.31 with a high free T4 (1.94), at a time your iron was paused. You noticed more worry and lighter sleep that winter.
insights.means: Your dose may have been effectively on the high side while iron was not competing with it. Your October TSH (2.71) was in range, so this has probably settled - a timed test will tell.
insights.do: At your next test, have the blood taken in the morning before your tablet, at the same lab as last time, with the time written down.
insights.expected: A clear answer on whether 50 mcg is right for you with iron in the picture. Tiredness, by contrast, is more often a sign of too little medicine or another cause.
insights.helps: A well-timed test shows whether your dose is right.

insights.title: Finding out why your thyroid slowed down
insights.found: Thyroid antibody tests (anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin) show whether hypothyroidism is autoimmune, the most common cause.
insights.why: Your record has no antibody result. Thyroid disease runs on both sides of your family (a maternal aunt and your paternal grandmother), and a cousin has coeliac disease, another autoimmune condition.
insights.means: Knowing the cause shapes how your thyroid is followed over time, what to watch for in pregnancy, and what your family may want to know.
insights.do: This is the first test in your personalised panel.
insights.expected: A clear cause for your hypothyroidism. Nearly all autoimmune hypothyroidism is antibody-positive.
insights.helps: One test tells you whether your thyroid condition is autoimmune.

insights.title: Your hair, skin and nails gummy may contain biotin
insights.found: Biotin, found in many hair, skin and nail supplements and some B-complex products, can make thyroid test results wrong.
insights.why: You take a hair, skin and nails gummy a few times a week, and these products usually contain biotin, often at high doses.
insights.means: A wrong result could lead to a dose change you don't need, or hide a real change.
insights.do: Check the label. If it contains biotin, stop it 2-3 days before your blood test, or tell the lab.
insights.helps: Avoids a falsely abnormal thyroid result.

insights.title: Simple causes of tiredness and hair shedding that haven't been checked
insights.found: Low iron, low B12 (about 1 in 4 people with hypothyroidism in a meta-analysis), low vitamin D and poor sleep all cause tiredness that thyroid treatment won't fix.
insights.why: You feel tired most afternoons, your hair has been shedding since spring and your nails break easily. You had iron-deficiency anaemia in 2024 and take vitamin D, with no recent levels on record.
insights.means: Part of your tiredness and hair shedding may have a simple, fixable cause.
insights.do: Your panel includes iron studies, B12, vitamin D and a full blood count. Hypothyroidism also puts you in a group where guidelines suggest a short sleep apnoea questionnaire (STOP-Bang) - it's free.
insights.expected: Either a fixable cause, or reassurance and a narrower search.
insights.helps: Checks the common, fixable causes of tiredness and hair shedding.

insights.title: Your wellbeing check-in
insights.found: Women treated for hypothyroidism report anxiety and low mood more often, even when their TSH is normal.
insights.why: Your answers give a PHQ-9 score of 5-6 (mild) and a GAD-7 score of 7-8 (mild). Stress is 5 out of 10, mostly work deadlines, alongside 45-50 hour weeks.
insights.means: What you feel is common and recognised. It is not caused by anything you did.
insights.do: Keep going with your therapist. We'll re-check with the standard questionnaires at your next assessment. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line straight away.
insights.expected: A clearer picture over time, alongside your care.
insights.helps: Gives you and your therapist a measurable starting point.

insights.title: Re-test 6 to 8 weeks after any dose or routine change
insights.found: Guidance is to check TSH 6 to 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine or changing the dose, then less often once it is at goal.
insights.why: Your iron has been paused and restarted, and you may move it to the evening. Each change can shift how much medicine you absorb, much like a dose change.
insights.means: A test taken too soon after a change can be misleading, and a test long after it may miss a swing.
insights.do: If you change when you take iron, magnesium or your tablet, ask your endocrinologist whether to bring your next TSH forward to 6-8 weeks later.
insights.helps: Times your tests so each result means something.

insights.title: Cervical screening every 5 years with an HPV test at your age
insights.found: Guidelines recommend cervical screening for women aged 30 to 65: an HPV test every 5 years, with or without a smear, or a smear alone every 3 years.
insights.why: You're 35, and you told us your last smear was in 2021. Screening isn't part of thyroid or iron care, so it's easy to miss.
insights.means: Screening finds early cell changes years before they could become cancer, when treatment is simple.
insights.do: If your last screen was a smear alone more than 3 years ago, book one with your doctor or gynaecologist. It takes a few minutes.
insights.expected: Most results are normal. If not, early follow-up is very effective.
insights.helps: Catches early changes years before they could matter.

insights.title: The HPV vaccine may still be worth discussing
insights.found: Catch-up HPV vaccination is routine up to age 26. From 27 to 45, guidelines recommend deciding together with your doctor.
insights.why: You're 35, and you don't know whether you had the vaccine.
insights.means: The benefit is smaller after 26, because many adults have already met the common HPV types, but it is not zero.
insights.do: Check your vaccination record, and ask your doctor whether it makes sense for you.
insights.expected: A shared decision, alongside regular screening.
insights.helps: A short conversation settles whether it's worth it for you.

insights.title: A tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough booster
insights.found: Adults who never had a Tdap dose should have one, then a tetanus booster every 10 years. A Tdap dose is also recommended in each pregnancy.
insights.why: Your last tetanus booster was in 2015, and you may try for a pregnancy.
insights.means: It keeps protection up, and whooping cough protection matters for anyone around newborns.
insights.do: Ask your doctor at your panel visit whether you are due, and remember the pregnancy dose if you conceive.
insights.expected: One injection covers you for about 10 years.
insights.helps: Ten years of protection from one injection.

insights.title: Occasional snoring: a free two-minute sleep questionnaire
insights.found: Guidelines suggest screening for obstructive sleep apnoea in people with relevant conditions, and hypothyroidism is on the list.
insights.why: Your partner has noticed you snore some nights, and you often wake unrefreshed after a full night.
insights.means: Most likely this is nothing serious, but sleep apnoea is a treatable cause of daytime tiredness.
insights.do: Answer the STOP-Bang questions in your panel questionnaires. A sleep study is only needed if the score is high.
insights.expected: Reassurance, or a clear next step.
insights.helps: Rules out a hidden cause of tiredness for free.

insights.title: Combination thyroid medicines are not routinely better
insights.found: Adding T3 (liothyronine) or using thyroid extract has not been shown to be consistently better than levothyroxine alone.
insights.why: You're on levothyroxine and still have afternoon tiredness and hair shedding, which can make other medicines sound appealing.
insights.means: The first steps are getting your tablet and iron timing right, steadying your dose, and checking other causes of your symptoms.
insights.do: Talk to your endocrinologist before trying anything else. Don't change medicines on your own.
insights.expected: Most people do well on levothyroxine once dose and timing are steady.
insights.helps: Saves you from switching medicines without a clear benefit.

insights.title: Past iron deficiency and a coeliac cousin: worth one blood test
insights.found: Autoimmune thyroid disease is linked with coeliac disease, autoimmune gastritis and type 1 diabetes. About 5 to 7% of people with it carry a coeliac antibody.
insights.why: You had iron-deficiency anaemia in 2024, a first cousin has coeliac disease, and we don't yet know if your hypothyroidism is autoimmune.
insights.means: These conditions can quietly reduce how well you absorb iron, B12 and your thyroid tablet.
insights.do: Ask your doctor whether a coeliac antibody test (tTG-IgA) should be added to your panel, before any change to your diet.
insights.expected: Most likely nothing is found. If something is, it is very treatable and can steady both your iron and your thyroid dose.
insights.helps: Knowing early can steady your iron, your dose and your energy.

insights.title: Your morning coffee may be too close to your tablet
insights.found: Coffee, dietary fibre and some foods reduce how much levothyroxine is absorbed when taken close to the tablet.
insights.why: You have your first coffee about 15 minutes after your tablet, and three coffees a day in total.
insights.means: Some mornings you may absorb less medicine than others, which adds to the swings in your results.
insights.do: Wait 30-60 minutes after your tablet before your first coffee, or ask your doctor about taking the tablet at bedtime instead.
insights.expected: Steadier absorption. No need to give up coffee, just move it.
insights.helps: Keep your coffee, move it by half an hour.

insights.title: A few more plant foods would help your heart in the long run
insights.found: Guidelines for all adults recommend plenty of vegetables, fruit, nuts, whole grains and lean protein, and fewer processed meats and refined carbohydrates.
insights.why: You eat 2 to 3 servings of fruit and vegetables a day, and takeaway lunches on most workdays. You have little red meat, which also matters for iron.
insights.means: Small changes now add up over decades for your heart, especially with high blood pressure in your family.
insights.do: Aim for 5 servings of fruit and vegetables, and include iron-rich foods such as lentils, beans and leafy greens with a source of vitamin C.
insights.expected: This is general heart-health advice, not specific to thyroid. Effects build over years.
insights.helps: Small changes now protect your heart and your iron for decades.

insights.title: More sleep on workdays may help your energy
insights.found: Studies link poorer or shorter sleep with an underactive thyroid. Which causes which is not known.
insights.why: You sleep about 6 to 6.5 hours on workdays and 8 or more at weekends, and wake around 4am a couple of nights a week.
insights.means: Regular, longer sleep is one of the easiest levers on your afternoon tiredness.
insights.do: Keep the same wake-up time every day, and move bedtime earlier by 20 minutes for a month. Note how you feel.
insights.expected: An association, not proof. It is low-risk and worth trying.
insights.helps: A free, low-risk lever on your daytime energy.

insights.title: Planning a pregnancy: plan your thyroid too
insights.found: Major guidelines agree an underactive thyroid should be well controlled before conception as well as during pregnancy.
insights.why: You told us you may try for a pregnancy in the next two years, and you have treated hypothyroidism.
insights.means: Thyroid needs usually rise early in pregnancy, so doctors plan the dose ahead. Iron and folate matter too.
insights.do: Tell your endocrinologist before you start trying, so they can plan your dose and tests.
insights.expected: With planning, outcomes are very good.
insights.helps: With planning, outcomes are very good.

ask.q: Why has my TSH moved so much?
ask.a: Your TSH was 12.9 at diagnosis in November 2024, still high in September 2025, then slightly low (0.31) in January 2026 while your iron was paused. It has been in range since June. The most likely reason is iron and coffee close to your tablet on some days and not others. A timed, same-lab test will help your doctor see where things stand now.

Your latest TSH (2.71 in October) is in range. In January it was low with a high free T4, which can mean a little too much, at a time your iron was paused. Your doctor decides the dose; a morning test before your tablet, at the same lab, gives them the clearest answer.

ask.q: When should I take my iron and magnesium?
ask.a: At least 4 hours away from your thyroid tablet. Many people take the tablet on waking and iron with dinner, with magnesium at night. Iron is absorbed better with a source of vitamin C and away from tea and coffee. Check with your doctor before changing.

ask.q: When should I take my thyroid tablet?
ask.a: With water, 30-60 minutes before breakfast and coffee, or at bedtime at least 3 hours after eating. Keep iron, magnesium and calcium at least 4 hours away. A systematic review found morning and bedtime equally effective. Check with your doctor before changing.

ask.q: Could my supplements affect my test results?
ask.a: Two ways: iron and magnesium near your tablet can reduce absorption, and biotin - common in hair, skin and nails gummies - can make thyroid test results wrong. Check the gummy label and stop it 2-3 days before blood tests if it contains biotin.

ask.q: Why am I tired in the afternoons?
ask.a: Tiredness with treated hypothyroidism is more often a sign of too little medicine or another cause than a side effect. Low iron, B12 or vitamin D, short sleep on workdays and possible sleep apnoea are common, fixable causes - none has been checked recently. Your panel covers them, plus a free sleep questionnaire.

Hair shedding and brittle nails are common after low iron stores and after thyroid levels swing, and both apply to you this year. Your panel checks ferritin and your thyroid together, which usually narrows it down. Shedding often settles a few months after the cause is fixed.

We can't calculate it yet, and we won't guess. The validated method needs 9 blood results you haven't had: albumin, creatinine, fasting glucose, CRP, a blood count (4 values) and ALP. They're all in your panel, so you'll see it at your next assessment.

ask.q: Do I really need the antibody test?
ask.a: It's the most useful new test for you. It shows whether your hypothyroidism is autoimmune, which shapes how it's followed, what to plan for in pregnancy and what your family may want to know.

ask.q: What does my mood score mean?
ask.a: Your answers give mild scores for both low mood and worry. These are screening scores, not a diagnosis. Anxiety and low mood are more common in treated hypothyroidism, and you're already working with a therapist, which is the right support.

Book your personalised panel - ideally with your thyroid test around 11 January, fasting, in the morning, before your tablet and with no iron for 24 hours. When the results arrive, every Mutanex analysis runs on them, your twin moves to version 2, and your doctor reviews a plan with you.

ask.q: Which vaccines or screening tests am I due?
ask.a: At 35, three things apply: cervical screening (an HPV test every 5 years, or a smear every 3), a conversation about whether the HPV vaccine is still worth it, and a Tdap booster if you are due - plus one in any pregnancy. None is about your thyroid, which is why they are easy to miss.

ask.q: I'm thinking about a pregnancy. What should I know?
ask.a: Tell your endocrinologist before you start trying. Thyroid needs usually rise early in pregnancy, so your dose and tests are planned ahead. Your antibody result, iron stores and a Tdap dose in pregnancy are all part of good preparation.

ask.q: Could my coffee be a problem?
ask.a: Not the coffee itself, but its timing. Coffee within 30-60 minutes of your tablet can reduce how much you absorb. You have your first one about 15 minutes after. Moving it by half an hour, or taking the tablet at bedtime, solves this.

ask.q: Which organs has my twin assessed?
ask.a: So far your thyroid, mind and mood, skin, hair and nails, and blood are assessed from your records and questionnaire; they are solid and coloured on your twin. Heart, kidneys, liver, pancreas, lungs, digestion, back and reproductive health are ghosted until your panel measures them.

ask.q: Should I ask for T3 or a different thyroid medicine?
ask.a: Combination medicines have not been shown to be consistently better than levothyroxine alone. The first steps are steady tablet and iron timing, the right dose and checking other causes of your symptoms. Discuss any change with your endocrinologist.

glossary: TSH
Thyroid-stimulating hormone. Made by the pituitary gland; high means your body wants more thyroid hormone.
Free T4 / Free T3
The thyroid hormones in your blood that are available to your body.
Levothyroxine
Your thyroid medicine: a copy of the hormone T4.
Anti-TPO
An antibody that shows whether a thyroid condition is autoimmune.
PHQ-9 / GAD-7
Short questionnaires that screen for low mood and worry. Not a diagnosis.
HbA1c
Your average blood sugar over about 3 months.
ApoB and Lp(a)
Markers of the particles that carry cholesterol into artery walls; Lp(a) is inherited and measured once.
hs-CRP
A sensitive marker of background inflammation.
Ferritin
A measure of your body's iron stores. It can read high during inflammation, so it is read with CRP.
Biological age
An estimate of how old your body seems from blood results, compared with your calendar age.
Evidence grade
How strong the research is: A strong, B good, C moderate, D early.
Digital twin
A model of your health built from your own records, which grows as new results arrive.

genes.function: Receptor for the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) or thyrotropin.
Sodium-independent transporter of chloride and iodide.
Acts as a substrate for the production of iodinated thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3).
Nuclear hormone receptor that can act as a repressor or activator of transcription.
Generates hydrogen peroxide which is required for the activity of thyroid peroxidase/TPO and lactoperoxidase/LPO.
Sodium:iodide symporter that mediates the transport of iodide into the thyroid gland.
Transcription factor that binds consensus sites on a variety of gene promoters and activate their transcription.
Seems to be a coreceptor in inhibin signaling, but seems not to be a high-affinity inhibin receptor.
Transcription factor involved in the specification of the lactotrope, somatotrope, and thyrotrope phenotypes in the developing anterior pituitary.
Transcription factor that binds and activates the promoter of thyroid specific genes such as thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase, and thyrotropin receptor.
Iodination and coupling of the hormonogenic tyrosines in thyroglobulin to yield the thyroid hormones T(3) and T(4).
Serine protease that suppresses hepcidin production, helping the body increase iron absorption when stores are low.
Cellular uptake of iron through receptor-mediated endocytosis of iron-loaded transferrin.
Exports iron from cells into the blood; its activity is controlled by hepcidin.

info_needed.why: They would establish whether the hypothyroidism is autoimmune. The status is currently unrecorded, and thyroid disease is reported on both sides of the family.

info_needed.item: Your thyroid results at diagnosis and your dose history
info_needed.why: These show whether the original diagnosis was overt or subclinical and whether the dose has ever been changed. The sources do not say which guideline recommendations apply.

info_needed.item: When you take your tablet, iron, magnesium and coffee
info_needed.why: Iron, magnesium and coffee near the dose reduce levothyroxine absorption; the timing in the record is self-reported and approximate.

info_needed.item: Ferritin, transferrin saturation and a blood count
info_needed.why: Iron-deficiency anaemia was treated in 2024, iron was later paused and restarted, and current iron stores are unknown.
Vitamin D is supplemented without a measured level, and B12 deficiency is more common in hypothyroidism.

info_needed.item: Whether you are planning a pregnancy, and when
info_needed.why: Pregnancy guidelines set different TSH targets and recommend planning the dose before conception.

info_needed.item: The cause of your 2024 anaemia, if one was found
info_needed.why: Heavy periods, diet or malabsorption such as coeliac disease each lead to different follow-up.

info_needed.item: Whether your gummy or other supplements contain biotin
info_needed.why: The ETA guideline lists biotin as a cause of immunoassay interference. Hair, skin and nail products often contain it.

info_needed.item: Your period pattern and how heavy your periods are
info_needed.why: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a common cause of iron deficiency in women and can recur.

info_needed.item: A coeliac antibody test, if you have had one
info_needed.why: Coeliac disease is more common with autoimmune thyroid disease and can cause iron deficiency and poor tablet absorption.

info_needed.item: Any other autoimmune condition you have had
info_needed.why: These could explain fatigue and other symptoms, and may support evaluating for autoimmune clustering.

info_needed.item: Snoring, pauses in breathing or morning headaches
info_needed.why: Hypothyroidism is listed as a comorbidity for which sleep apnoea screening is recommended.

info_needed.item: A doctor's examination of your thyroid
info_needed.why: Guidelines recommend examining the gland; a goitre or nodule changes the next steps.

info_needed.item: How your hair shedding has changed over time
info_needed.why: Shedding that began after a known trigger and is settling needs less investigation than shedding that is getting worse.

F8.statement: Nearly all spontaneous (presumed autoimmune) primary overt hypothyroidism is antibody-positive, and TPOAb is more often detectable than TgAb. A TPOAb result would therefore mainly confirm or refute an autoimmune etiology rather than redirect therapy.
F8.limitations: Etiologic classification is not the same as a management change. The data are from untreated or newly diagnosed patients in older studies and assays. TPOAb-negative autoimmune disease can occur because TgAb exists as an alternative marker.
F8.population: Adults with newly diagnosed primary overt hypothyroidism in a population cohort; older reference-style reviews

F4.statement: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis and celiac disease are the autoimmune conditions most specifically linked with autoimmune thyroiditis. They can present with anaemia, micronutrient deficiency and impaired absorption of oral drugs. Parietal cell antibodies were the most common organ-specific autoantibody in a large ATD cohort, followed by GADA.
F4.limitations: Mostly narrative review and prevalence data. Autoantibody prevalence is not the same as clinical disease. The sources do not show that antibody screening improves outcomes. The patient is younger than the cohort.
F4.population: Adults with Hashimoto's thyroiditis or other autoimmune thyroid disease. The cohort was 1502 Italian patients, mostly women with a mean age of about 53.

F14.statement: Levothyroxine-treated hypothyroid women with normalised TSH had a higher prevalence of anxiety and depression than women without hypothyroidism in a Spanish case-control study. This is an association only.
F14.limitations: Case-control design with convenience sampling and an online self-report questionnaire (HADS). Causation and temporality cannot be established. Fatigue and sleepiness were not assessed. The mean age is close to the patient's, but the sample comes from one region. Only a narrow TSH range was included.
F14.population: Spanish primary-care women (mean age about 35) with primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine for at least 6 months and TSH 0.4-4.0 mIU/L, versus women without thyroid disease.

F9.statement: Biotin supplementation is a documented cause of analytical interference in streptavidin-biotin-based immunoassays, the formats commonly used for thyroid hormone measurement. It can produce false positive or false negative results and a seemingly coherent but spurious hormonal profile, including a false biochemical picture of hyperthyroidism.
F9.limitations: Narrative review abstract only. The excerpt gives no prevalence, no assay-by-assay susceptibility and no biotin intake thresholds. Whether a given TSH, FT4 or FT3 assay uses streptavidin-biotin chemistry is not stated for this patient.
F9.population: General patients undergoing immunoassay-based hormone testing; not specific to hypothyroidism or to this patient.

F10.statement: Thyroid function immunoassays (TSH, free T4, free T3) are vulnerable to six main interference types: macro-TSH, biotin, anti-streptavidin antibodies, anti-ruthenium antibodies, thyroid hormone autoantibodies and heterophilic antibodies. Reported interferences often led to misdiagnosis or inappropriate management. Suspicion should be raised when clinical and biochemical findings are discordant, and identification relies on additional laboratory work-up.
F10.limitations: Review of reported cases, so subject to reporting bias. The sources list no supplement other than biotin among the six interference types.
F10.population: Patients undergoing thyroid function testing; case-report-derived data (more than 150 patients).

F25.statement:
A descriptive review of major guidelines (Endocrine Society, ETA, RANZCOG, ATA, ACOG) found agreement on several points:
- Overt hypothyroidism should be treated during pregnancy and also before conception, with similar management and treatment targets.
- Universal screening is discouraged, and targeted TSH screening of high-risk patients is supported.

The 2026 ATA guideline provides updated recommendations on thyroid function testing and hypothyroidism management across preconception, pregnancy and postpartum. Its specific recommendations were not in the supplied abstract.
F25.limitations: The ATA 2026 recommendation tables were not supplied. The guideline comparison is a descriptive narrative review. Exact surveillance intervals and targets cannot be extracted from these sources.
F25.population: Women with thyroid disease before, during and after pregnancy

F24.population: Adults with subclinical hypothyroidism versus healthy controls (8 studies; 2916 patients with subclinical hypothyroidism); treatment status not described in the abstract.

F11.statement: In a systematic review and meta-analysis, patients with hypothyroidism had lower serum B12 than healthy participants and a pooled B12 deficiency frequency of about 27%. The pooled AITD estimate was 18%, but pooled B12 levels in AITD did not differ significantly from healthy controls.

F11.population: Adults and mixed-age patients with thyroid disorders across 64 studies (n=28597); Asian and European subgroups differed.

F5.statement: A systematic review of 12 studies found that levothyroxine at replacement doses had a very low risk of cardiac, neuropsychiatric and musculoskeletal adverse events. Adverse events occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed, and blinded placebo-controlled trials in euthyroid patients showed no significant differences. Some subjective symptoms may be placebo or nocebo effects.
F5.limitations: Only 12 heterogeneous studies; most comparisons were underpowered with wide confidence intervals. Several RCTs were unregistered. Anxiety was one of several pooled neuropsychiatric outcomes. The excerpt does not show anxiety-specific results. Not specific to women in their thirties.
F5.population: Mostly adults with hypothyroidism or subclinical hypothyroidism (mean ages 14-93 years across studies). The review's most explicit anxiety data come from studies of suppressive or supraphysiologic dosing. Anxiety was one of many outcomes.

F6.statement: A systematic review found that adverse events attributed to levothyroxine, including neuropsychiatric events such as headache, occurred mainly when TSH was suppressed. In euthyroid patients in blinded placebo-controlled trials there was no significant difference. The pattern suggests thyroid status (over-replacement versus normal TSH) is the main discriminator for a drug-related headache.
F6.limitations: Small, heterogeneous studies. Headache-specific results are in sections not shown in the excerpt. Mostly not powered for headache. Findings are associations, and the excerpt does not show whether headache itself differed by group.
F6.population: Mixed populations (12 studies, n=1817), mostly hypothyroid or subclinical hypothyroid patients, plus patients on TSH-suppressive therapy.

F13.statement: Hypothyroidism can plausibly account for fatigue and dry skin, but its symptoms are non-specific. No single symptom reliably identifies thyroid disease, and persistent symptoms in levothyroxine-treated patients are hard to attribute to thyroid status. This supports checking whether current thyroid replacement is biochemically adequate while keeping non-thyroid causes open.
F13.limitations: The review is narrative. The case-control study addressed untreated, newly diagnosed overt disease, not treated patients. The sources do not address a 35-year-old woman on stable levothyroxine.

F7.statement: A narrative review states that TSH should be monitored 6 to 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine or changing the dose, to avoid over- or under-treatment. This defines a standard biochemical checkpoint against which new or changing symptoms can be assessed. It does not describe anxiety trajectories.
F7.limitations: Narrative review; it addresses TSH monitoring, not symptom timing. Applicability to a young woman with possible autoimmune hypothyroidism is not specified.

sources.title: Hypothyroidism: A Review.
sources.quote: Thyrotropin monitoring should be performed 6 to 8 weeks after initiating levothyroxine treatment, or when changing the dose, and then annually once the thyrotropin level…

F12.statement: The guideline recommends OSA screening for high-risk individuals with typical symptoms, signs or relevant comorbidities. Hypothyroidism is listed as a relevant comorbidity, and anxiety appears in the same list. Routine screening is not recommended for people without high-risk features.
F12.limitations: This is a Chinese national guideline and only the abstract was provided. The evidence base behind each grade was not shown.
